newsitem.title: USA: For Native Americans, gaming is not the only business.
newsitem.headline: For Native Americans, gaming is not the only business.

text.p: The growth of casino gambling on Indian reservations has buoyed the economies of many Indian communities, but Indian business advocates say what's really needed is more entrepreneurship.
They target ventures linking non-Indian businesses with new Indian entrepreneurs, as well as more investment by successful Indian-owned businesses in new enterprises.

Links between non-Indian businesses and Indian entrepreneurs would not just be philanthropic, but offer business opportunities to both sides, says Veronica Tiller, an Indian historian and consultant who has produced a reference guide to doing business with what she calls Indian Country.

"What I see here is that while there is a growing desire -- and a trend toward developing the private sector both on and off the reservation -- there is a real need for joint ventures with people who have business experience," she said. "Indian people do not have that experience. We've always had an economy, but it was not the type we have today."
Tiller says there are numerous opportunities for small businesses on or near reservations such as coin-operated laundries, gas stations and retailers, as well as manufacturing and service companies.
"The things that exist all over America -- those opportunities exist on Indian Country," she said.
The federal government, attempting to bolster business ties with Indians, offers several tax incentives that make doing business with Indian partners advantageous.

For example, tribes and tribal-owned corporations are not subject to federal income tax for on-reservation joint businesses. Thus, a joint venture structured as a limited partnership or limited corporation could allocate the tribe's share of tax deductions and credits to the venture, according to Joseph Pluchinota, an Albuquerque, N.M., consultant whose company provides training for tribal organisations.

In addition, federal excise taxes may be sheltered for the venture, and tribes can utilize tax-exempt financing and other tax-exempt obligations, he wrote in the autumn issue of the periodical Winds of Change. Businesses located on Indian land also benefit from accelerated depreciation for facilities and incremental wage credits against income tax for certain wage earners and insurance costs, and a tribal venture may be exempt from state and local gross-receipt taxes.

Since a tribal work force is likely underutilized and non-union, Pluchinota said training and human resource development funding may be available to enhance workers' skills. At the same time, though, he cautioned that "the cross-cultural challenges between workers, policy-makers and others are many," which is not a factor to be ignored.
Aside from the tax benefits, Tiller said there are pure business opportunities in forming alliances with Indian tribes or individual entrepreneurs.
She notes that 36 states have Indian tribes and the majority of those states also have some form of gaming. That means the tribes have means of financing new ventures.

"Many more Indian people are looking at the possibility of establishing their own businesses," Tiller said. "Many of the large communities are located near large metropolitan areas. In Minnesota, there are tribes located near both Minneapolis and St. Paul. There are thousands of businesses and business opportunities within those areas."

Numerous American Indian chambers of commerce and business associations across the country are dedicated to encouraging Indian-owned businesses. Some focus primarily on tribe-owned enterprises, some on recruiting non-Indian businesses to tribal ventures, and others work more on bringing jobs to reservations by persuading big business to establish operations nearby.

"There certainly are a lot of opportunities out there for the tribes if they decide that's what they want to do," said Dennis Dowell, project director at the Native American Business Development Centre in Tulsa, Okla. "But generally the tribes don't think in terms of small operations they can assist," he said. "They think in terms of providing many jobs, much larger in scope."

Peter Homer, of the National Indian Business Association in Washington, D.C., said his group hopes to identify successful Native American-owned companies off reservations and entice them to move their companies -- or branches of them -- back to the reservations.

"We have some (Indian) millionaires in this country and they have wonderful big businesses. If you give them an incentive, they will go back on Indian reservations and establish businesses with the tribal governments," he said.
"I don't say 'Go back. Go in partnership with the tribe and with other people,'" Homer said. "The Indian tribes can't depend on non-Indians -- Indians are going to have to do it for themselves."

He notes that of the nearly 100 Indian-owned casinos, most are doing well and can provide funding for small businesses that banks would otherwise not provide. "What's good about that is that most of the casinos are turning the profits into grants for small businesses on the Indian reservations so they can keep the money on the reservations.
"That is going to create an economic base in the next 10 years if it continues to be profitable."

Tiller has compiled a study of the nation's 574 Indian reservations and communities that is regarded as an authoritative reference on Indian business and industry. The 714-page volume, "Tiller's Guide to Indian Country", can be browsed on the Internet at http:www.rt66.com/(tilde)vetiller/ and can be ordered from Tiller's BowArrow Publishing in Albuquerque at 800-895-8668.
